books.title: So Good They Can't Ignore You
books.author: Cal Newport
books.description: Why "follow your passion" is bad career advice, and what works instead.
ideas: Passion follows mastery
Most people don't discover a pre-existing passion. They become passionate about work they've become very good at.
Career capital
Rare and valuable skills are the currency you trade for great jobs: autonomy, creativity and impact.
The craftsman mindset
Focus on what value you can offer, not on what the job offers you. Getting better is the path to loving your work.
Deliberate practice
Getting better requires stretching beyond comfort, with feedback. Coasting at what you already know builds no capital.

books.title: Range
books.author: David Epstein
books.description: Why generalists often triumph in a world that celebrates early specialization.
ideas: Kind and wicked learning environments
Chess and golf have clear rules and fast feedback, so early specialization works. Most of life is messier, and broad experience helps more.
The sampling period
Many top performers tried several activities before settling. Exploring helps you find a good match, which matters more than an early start.
Analogical thinking
People with broad experience can borrow solutions from unrelated fields. Outsiders often solve problems that insiders are stuck on.
Late starters aren't behind
Switching paths isn't wasted time. What you learned elsewhere often becomes an unusual advantage.

books.title: Designing Your Life
books.author: Bill Burnett & Dave Evans
books.description: Two Stanford designers apply design thinking to building a career and life you love.
ideas: Prototype your career
Before making a big change, test it in small ways: talk to people in the field, shadow someone, take a short project.
Odyssey plans
Sketch three different five-year lives: your current path, what you'd do if that disappeared, and what you'd do if money and judgment didn't matter.
Gravity problems
Some problems can't be solved, like gravity. Accept them and design around them instead of wasting energy fighting.
Track your energy
For a few weeks, note which activities energize or drain you. The patterns reveal what work fits you.

books.title: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People
books.author: Stephen R. Covey
books.description: A principle-centred approach to personal and professional effectiveness.
ideas: Be proactive
Between what happens and how you respond, there's a space. Focus on what you can influence rather than what you can't.
Begin with the end in mind
Picture what you want people to say about you at the end of your life. Let that vision guide your daily choices.
Put first things first
Important but not urgent activities, like planning, relationships and health, are where real effectiveness lies. Schedule them before urgent trivia.
Seek first to understand
Most people listen with the intent to reply. Listen to understand first, and you'll be understood more easily.
Sharpen the saw
Regularly renew your body, mind, relationships and spirit. Without maintenance, effectiveness wears down.

books.title: Grit
books.author: Angela Duckworth
books.description: Research showing that passion and perseverance often matter more than talent.
ideas: Effort counts twice
Talent times effort equals skill; skill times effort equals achievement. Effort shows up in both steps.
Grit is passion plus perseverance
Gritty people stick with long-term goals for years, through setbacks and boredom.
Interest comes first
Passion usually starts with a spark of interest, then grows through practice and finding purpose.
Hope as a habit
Gritty people expect their efforts to improve their future. That optimism keeps them trying after failures.
